item.title: Improving CoT Monitorability of Evaluation Awareness via Verbalization Training
item.description:
This is joint work with Sahar Abdelnabi and David Krueger. It is mostly a linkpost for the paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36316) but also contains some additional commentary on CoT monitorability.

TL;DR: Verbalization training makes a model less reticent about verbalizing a belief it already holds. We apply it to evaluation awareness and show that VT-induced verbalizations track the underlying belief: independently implanting evaluation knowledge through synthetic-document fine-tuning produces corresponding qualitative changes in the content of the model's verbalizations (see “A Causal Test: Does Trained Verbalization Track Implanted Awareness?” below). Across three models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Kimi K2.6, and Inkling) VT increases verbalized evaluation awareness by 2.4--2.9x, including in held-out agentic settings. At the same time, the VT-trained models' ability to recognize evaluations and their task behavior remain largely stable.

More broadly, we think reporting propensity is a useful target for both measuring and improving on CoT monitorability. Models possess safety-relevant information that they only sometimes expose in chain of thought. Finding ways to train them to report this information more often would likely be critical for chain-of-thought monitorability. However, doing this naively is risky and we need smart training methods that avoid harmful side effects (e.g., reducing trustworthiness of verbalizations done in CoT). VT is an initial attempt to intervene on reporting while limiting those failure modes.

Summary

    • Verbalized evaluation awareness is a high-precision but low-recall measure for evaluation awareness. Explicit evaluation-awareness reasoning is useful evidence that a model suspects it is being evaluated. But the absence of such reasoning is hard to interpret: a model may recognize an evaluation without saying so.
    • VT uses a model's own spontaneous verbalizations to locate moments at which the relevant belief is likely already present. We collect rollouts in which the base model mentions being evaluated, truncate each rollout immediately before that mention, and train the model to verbalize from these frozen prefixes.
    • To ensure VT does not lead to confabulations and amplification of behaviors correlated (but not causally linked with) evaluation awareness, we use a span-masked RL objective where reward and KL regularization apply only to the tokens in the evaluation-awareness verbalization. Tokens outside that span, and entirely non-verbalizing continuations, receive no gradient. The aim is to train the reporting decision without directly reinforcing the formation of evaluation awareness or correlated task behavior.
    • Across 17 evaluation-awareness conditions and three models, verbalized evaluation awareness increases in all 51 model-condition comparisons. Average in-distribution rates (on EAB) rise from 5.8% to 16.7% for Qwen, 17.7% to 41.6% for Inkling, and 24.8% to 61.9% for Kimi.
    • The effect transfers to OOD agentic evaluations. For example, verbalized evaluation awareness on Agentic Misalignment rises from 5.1% to 36.8% for Qwen, 23.3% to 57.1% for Inkling, and 60.1% to 88.3% for Kimi.
    • We do not detect a meaningful improvement in the models' ability to distinguish evaluation from deployment contexts. We also find little change in task compliance, harmfulness conditional on compliance, or general-language perplexity.
    • Through various ablations, we show that the details of the objective matter. Without span masking, training barely increases verbalization. Without KL regularization, it produces uncontrolled amplification and behavioral drift. Removing both produces output degeneration.
    • To test whether VT teaches the model to generate generic evaluation-related language or instead tracks the relevant latent belief, we independently fine-tune a model on synthetic documents containing richer knowledge about safety evaluations, then compose this intervention with VT. The resulting verbalizations reflect the newly implanted knowledge: they identify what the evaluation is testing and how the model would pass or fail it. This provides evidence that VT exposes information available to the model rather than merely installing a canned phrase.

Introduction

Evaluation awareness is clearly becoming a major issue in model auditing. But we still do not have any good instruments for measuring it. White-box techniques such as Natural Language Autoencoders and contrastive probes can work well in synthetic settings, but existing methods generalize poorly to realistic evaluation contexts, often disagree with one another, and correlate only weakly with spontaneous verbalized evaluation awareness (Claude Fable 5 & Claude Mythos 5 System Card, pp. 188–190). Consequently, neither a positive nor a negative reading from these tools can currently be treated as decisive evidence that a model is evaluation-aware. White-box methods also require weight access, ruling out their use by external auditors, academics, and users of closed-weight frontier models.

Verbalizations of evaluation awareness are different. They are relatively clear and trustworthy evidence that the model suspects it is being evaluated [footnote, in principle you could object that we do not have a way to verify faithfulness of these verbalizations, but this seems unlikely to me as it is not clear to me why LLMs would learn to misreport evaluation awareness]. But the converse does not hold: a lack of verbalization is hard to interpret, because a model may recognize an evaluation and act differently without saying so. In other words, verbalized evaluation awareness (VEA) appears to have high precision but low recall.

Worse, this recall problem may be getting more severe. Recent frontier models verbalize evaluation awareness drastically less often even as their ability to recognize evaluations improves. In a UK AISI evaluation, when asked after an interaction whether it was an evaluation, Opus 4.6 identified it correctly 45.5% of the time, up from 12.5% for Opus 4.5. Yet Opus 4.6 spontaneously mentioned being evaluated in only 2.3% of interactions, down from 11.0% for Opus 4.5 (Claude Opus 4.6 System Card, pp. 117--118). Apollo reports a similar cross-generation drop for OpenAI models: GPT-5.6 verbalizes evaluation awareness in 16% of samples, compared with 43% for GPT-5.5 (GPT-5.6 System Card).

On the whole, the situation is precarious: latent tools remain unreliable in either direction, while the higher-precision verbalization signal has low and potentially declining recall. A natural question that we investigate is whether we could train LLMs to verbalize evaluation awareness more often.

Verbalization Training

Why is training LLMs to verbalize a latent belief challenging?

There are two main challenges:

First, we need a reliable supervision signal. We would like to reward a model for verbalizing evaluation awareness only when it is actually evaluation-aware. But this requires knowing both which rollouts contain evaluation awareness and where within those rollouts the awareness is present. Both are latent properties with no accessible ground truth.

The second is designing a credit assignment scheme so that training rewards only verbalization, and not the underlying belief or other correlated behaviors.

In this work, we introduce verbalization training (VT), which addresses both these challenges.

VT leverages the model's own spontaneous but potentially rare verbalizations of EA as evidence of when the relevant belief is present, both at the rollout level and within a rollout.

To solve the credit assignment problem, we propose a KL-regularized RL update that applies only when the model verbalizes EA, and only on the tokens of the verbalization span. By using the model's own spontaneous verbalization as the indicator of when the belief is present, we ensure that our method never rewards the model for verbalizing EA when the belief has not actually formed. And because reward only applies inside the verbalization span, training pressure cannot reinforce belief formation or correlated behaviors outside the verbalization span.

Method

There are two clever bits in verbalization training. First, we solve the supervision signal problem by observing that a model's rare spontaneous verbalizations can serve as their own supervision signal. The verbalization is evidence that evaluation awareness was present immediately before the model initiated the verbalization. Second, for the credit-assignment problem, we use KL regularization to make it costly for the model to confabulate verbalizations and use masking to limit effects on unrelated verbalizations or behaviors within a rollout.

Concretely, VT operates in two stages. The first is a data-collection stage in which we sample rollouts from the base model and use an LLM judge to identify spontaneous evaluation-awareness verbalizations. For every positive rollout, the judge also identifies the precise span containing the verbalization. We then truncate the rollout immediately before the first token in that span. The original prompt and all preceding reasoning are frozen. We call these witnessed prefixes: the model's own continuation has witnessed that evaluation awareness can be present at that exact point. This of course relies on the assumption that spontaneous, explicit evaluation-awareness statements are usually sincere enough that they provide high-precision positive examples. Crucially, however, we never need to label the much harder negative cases. We do not assume that a silent rollout is evaluation-unaware.

The second is the training stage. We generally construct a seed dataset of around 500 prefixes. Starting from each frozen prefix, we sample new continuations. A continuation receives reward if it contains an evaluation-awareness verbalization.

Objective: We assume access to a judge that, given a rollout , returns both a verbalization label and, when , the token spans containing the verbalization. Let denote the union of these span-token positions. If the rollout contains no verbalization, it receives no reward and does not contribute to the update. Otherwise, each detected verbalization span receives a reward of . Both the policy-gradient update and KL penalty are restricted to tokens in .

Here, is a policy-gradient surrogate at token for the binary verbalization reward .

We show in the paper that this objective is equivalent to amplifying the model's propensity to verbalize in a given context by a multiplicative factor. At the prompt or dataset level, this gives the following amplification law:

where is the probability of at least one evaluation-awareness verbalization and is the amplification factor.

What does the KL penalty do?

KL acts as a counterweight to the verbalization reward and ensures that the model cannot obtain it by verbalizing indiscriminately. Specifically, the model must pay a KL cost to increase the probability of verbalizing. Loosely speaking, this cost increases with how unlikely the base model was to verbalize in that context. For example, when the model lacks the relevant belief, producing a verbalization is likely to incur a substantial KL cost. The KL penalty also helps prevent reward hacking of the LLM judge by penalizing unlikely ways of phrasing a report, thereby discouraging newly invented, judge-optimized verbalizations.

What does masking do?

Both the verbalization reward and KL penalty are restricted to the verbalization span:

    • Tokens inside a detected verbalization receive the reward and KL gradients.
    • Tokens outside the span receive no gradient.
    • A continuation with no detected verbalization receives no gradient at all.

Masking keeps credit assignment local. When a continuation contains no verbalization, there is no relevant span to target, so we apply no gradient. Penalizing the whole continuation for not verbalizing would provide a diffuse signal that could alter unrelated reasoning or behavior. When a continuation does contain a verbalization, the gradients apply only to that span, preventing training from reinforcing other behaviors that merely happen to correlate with verbalization. Masking also keeps the reward and KL penalty balanced: the verbalization reward is sparse and bounded, whereas an unmasked KL penalty accumulates across every token in a long continuation and can overwhelm the reward. Applying both signals only to the verbalization span allows KL to constrain changes to the report without preventing the model from learning to verbalize.

In the paper, we analyze several objective variants and show that masking and KL both play crucial roles in ensuring that learning remains efficient and that the resulting verbalizations remain calibrated and trustworthy.

Empirically, we observe that removing masking makes learning extremely weak, while removing KL results in a highly miscalibrated, and likely confabulating, model.

Results

Models: We use Tinker to fine-tune three models:

    • Qwen3.6-35B-A3B;
    • Kimi K2.6; and
    • Inkling.

Datasets: For our experiments, we primarily use EvalAwareBench (EAB). EAB contains 100 base safety prompts derived from HarmBench. It renders each prompt with one or more of eight independently toggleable cues that may trigger evaluation awareness, such as prose register, ecological completeness, or implicit evaluation disclosure. Any subset of these cues can be enabled, providing a large set of prompts with different types and degrees of artificiality. Importantly, a prompt looking less realistic does not necessarily mean that a model will recognize it as an evaluation or verbalize that recognition: evaluation awareness is strongly model-dependent.

We use two sets of EAB conditions. The single-factor set applies each of the eight cues separately, producing eight versions of every base prompt. The nested set begins with the naturalistic prompt and cumulatively adds cues until all eight are present, producing nine more versions. This gives us 17 evaluation-awareness conditions in total.

Training details overview: To construct the training data, we first evaluated each of EAB's eight factors separately under the base policy and selected the factor with the highest spontaneous VEA rate. This was F8 for Qwen and F2 for Kimi and Inkling. F8 explicitly discloses the evaluative context through references to testing, grading, or scoring. F2 instead signals that the scenario is artificially constructed through internal inconsistencies, implausibly convenient setups, or suspiciously detailed task descriptions. For each model, we randomly selected 50 prompts from its chosen factor and sampled generations until we accumulated 500 VEA-positive rollouts. These became the witnessed prefixes used for training. We then evaluated the trained models on all 100 prompts across all 17 EAB conditions, as well as three held-out agentic settings. We perform 200 steps of training for Qwen and Inkling and 100 steps for Kimi.

The training data came from one evaluation-awareness condition per model, so this shows generalization across both prompts and combinations of evaluation cues. The gains also approximately followed the functional form predicted above. Fitting one amplification factor per model gives values between 3.08 and 3.73 with root-mean-square (RMS) differences of 8.2–10.1 percentage points across EvalAwareBench conditions, and of 2.4–15.1 percentage points on the held-out agentic evaluations.


VT transfers to OOD agentic evaluations

EAB is a conversational dataset. To check whether VT generalizes, we evaluated the trained policies on Agentic Misalignment and on the harmful and benign splits of AgentHarm. We find that transfer is good and also quite well-calibrated (RMS of 2.4–15.1 pp for all three models).

A Causal Test: Does Trained Verbalization Track Implanted Evaluation Meta-Knowledge?

Deckenbach et al. show that synthetic document finetuning (SDF) on documents containing meta-knowledge about safety evaluations, e.g., conflicting goals or ethical dilemmas, causes LLMs to behave differently on evaluation benchmarks without verbalizing the awareness responsible for this change.

We replicate this intervention on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B using the authors' corpus and training protocol, and then compose the SDF LoRA with the independently trained VT LoRA. We evaluate the resulting SDF+VT policy across EvalAwareBench, Agentic Misalignment, and the harmful and benign AgentHarm splits. We focus the analysis below on harmful AgentHarm because it directly instantiates one of the facts taught by SDF: safety evaluations use harmful requests to test safeguards and refusal.

As shown in the table below, the SDF+VT model verbalizes evaluation awareness at a considerably higher rate than the SDF model alone. More notably, we found that the SDF+VT model's verbalizations are qualitatively different from those of the VT model alone and reflect the enhanced knowledge that the SDF-trained model has.

This is strong evidence that VT does not merely teach the model to emit generic evaluation-related language, but rather tracks the model's latent knowledge and beliefs about evaluation. To quantify this shift in verbalization content, we use GPT-5.6-Luna to score verbalizations from different policies on two aspects. Target Recovery tracks whether the verbalization correctly identifies the purpose of the evaluation, while Pass Condition tracks whether it correctly infers that harmful compliance would fail the evaluation or that preserving safeguards and refusing would pass.

VT does not appear to improve evaluation recognition or meaningfully change behavior

VT raises two concerns:

    1. It may change the "actual" evaluation awareness, i.e., LLM may get better at evaluation recognition.
    2. It may change behavior in unwanted way or impose some sort of "alignment tax".

For the first, we show in the paper that models do not get better at a black-box evaluation-identification task in which a model reads a completed transcript and estimates whether it came from evaluation or deployment. Similarly, for Qwen, we show that scores for a contrastive probe do not change in any meaningful way.

For the second, we conduct extensive testing. Across the eight single-factor EvalAwareBench conditions, average task-compliance changes are +0.6 percentage points for Qwen and -0.1 points for both Kimi and Inkling. The largest absolute change in any individual condition is 2.4, 1.6, and 1.4 points respectively. Binary compliance could miss subtler changes in harmfulness, so we additionally score responses using the StrongREJECT rubric, both across all responses and conditional on task compliance. Again, changes for the fully trained models are small. On the whole, we are quite confident that the VT trained models have essentially the same behavior profile as the original models.

Ablations

Our ablations produced distinct failure modes:

    • No span masking, with KL: training barely learns. The reward for a short verbalization has to compete with KL accumulated over the full continuation.
    • Span masking, without KL: VEA on the training prompts nearly saturates, but transfer becomes miscalibrated and task behavior shifts.
    • Neither masking nor KL: outputs degenerate, the model emits repeated VEA spans, and measured latent evaluation awareness and behavior drift.
    • Supervised fine-tuning instead of RL: VEA increases on the training distribution but transfers weakly to held-out agentic settings.
    • Starting from prompts rather than witnessed prefixes: the model shows more signs of overfitting, such as producing multiple evaluation-awareness spans in one rollout.

Discussion: Reporting Propensity as a Lever for CoT Monitorability

Until now, CoT monitorability cases have been built on absence of capability to control CoT and perform substantial reasoning without CoT. But Astra / Fable class models are already showing that such incapability cases are insufficient. This naturally means that we would be relying more on a propensity-based safety case. I think in this context, it would be really useful to know what kind of (latent) knowledge we want model to have high propensity of verbalizing, and to specifically train and manipulate this propensity. I am quite excited about VT in this context.

In this work, our focus has been on evaluation awareness[1], but the method is not intrinsically about evaluation awareness. It applies whenever:

    1. a model sometimes holds safety-relevant information;
    2. it occasionally verbalizes that information spontaneously; and
    3. those spontaneous reports are precise enough to identify belief-positive prefixes.

Possible targets include awareness of control measures[2], suspicious instructions, prefilled reasoning, hidden objectives, or opportunities to exploit an oversight mechanism. If a model's misbehavior depends on such information, increasing the probability that the model reports it could make the behavior easier to detect and understand. In general, verbalization training could become one ingredient in maintaining CoT monitorability as model generations become more reticent.

Open Questions and Future Work

(If you work on any of these, I would be interested in learning about your efforts and potentially might be interested in collaborating! )

Understanding and Extending VT

What is the safe amplification range? Theoretically, you could keep on amplifying VEA by repeating VT, but in practice there is likely to be some limit to this that we should try to understand. In the paper, we do a second round of VT on Inkling that compounds the gains but it does increase the behavioural drift. Understanding how far reporting propensity can be amplified before trustworthiness deteriorates is an important next step.

Applying VT to other 'known' (mis)behaviors. VT is a pretty general method. I would be excited about people applying this to improve monitorability of other "known" (mis)behaviors, like user awareness or control awareness or prefill awareness or even something like self-incrimination. I don't think these applications are totally trivial (e.g., user awareness in Transluce setup is installed externally via planting information in system prompt due to which it is unclear how to localize this 'belief') so there are research problems to solve here too. I expect this might help us better understand the contexts in which VT does, and does not, work.

How to deal with the case of LLM whose verbalization rate is literally zero (e.g., GPT-OSS models)? I am not convinced that these models are totally EA unaware. How can we construct the seed dataset in such a case? Could you do something like "seeding training round" where you first train against labels from NLAs / probes and then once there are sufficient verbalizations, use VT? In such a case, likely the initial seed dataset for VT would not contain fully faithful verbalizations; does VT still work fine in this case or not?

Mechanistic understanding of the LoRA adapters. I have uploaded the LoRA adapters (in Tinker's native format) here. I would love for people to try and do mech interp on them to understand what VT is actually learning.

On Understanding Evaluation Awareness and Friends

Using VT models' verbalizations to better understand "space" of evaluation awareness. My vague sense is that EA is basically the wrong "frame". There are loose notions defined such as frame awareness and meta-gaming that attempt to broaden evaluation awareness but I am not convinced yet that any of these are the right notions from a model's perspective. In other words, I don't think EA / frame-awareness / meta-gaming are atomic enough concepts and this is perhaps one reason why we are struggling with measuring and intervening this phenomenon. I would love to see more conceptual work on clarifying this. Relatedly, it is surprising to me that most "verbalizations" of EA are benign; that is they don't lead to eval gaming. It would be cool to have some sense of what differentiates passive EA and active eval gaming in frontier LLMs.

See this nice initial analysis done by 'Lumen' a GPT-6-Astra model instance: https://uzman-anwar.github.io/verbalization-training/wildchat-taxonomy.html

Develop "hybrid" probes for EA. There are sort of two probe designs for EA in literature: contrastive probes from Hua et al. that Anthropic uses and verbalization-supervised probes from Abdelnabi et al.. A cool mini-project could be to understand how these probes "differ" and could we do some sort of hybrid probe that would be better than both?


  1. ^

    Evaluation awareness is a particularly nice target here because the "drop" in verbalization of EA is perhaps very similar to the kind of drop we should expect for other pieces of knowledge that LLMs currently do verbalize in their CoT.

  2. ^

    Reticent to verbalize a belief also exists in post-hoc answering. My vague sense is that we are likely currently underestimating control awareness in LLMs due to this.

item.title: How to change your identity. A guide to the highest leverage behavior change technique.
item.description:
According to Atomic Habits, changing your identity is the highest leverage way to improve your habits, but nobody tells you how to do it.

Don’t say “I’m trying to quit smoking.” Say “I’m not a smoker”. Don’t say “I’m trying to lose weight.” Say “I’m a health nut.”

All well and good. But how do you practically do this, aside from stating your new identity? I’ve worked on developing the approach further and had a lot of success with these techniques.

And changing your identity is especially great because it creates "passive happiness". You do the work once and it lasts a lifetime with little to no maintenance.

Using these techniques I’ve successfully:

  • Stopped being bothered by mosquitoes.
  • Become able to wait patiently for food instead of freaking out when it's late.
  • Learned to like the rain while living in Vancouver and London.
  • Become a tough person instead of someone derailed by the smallest amount of pain.

All by doing what I call identity work.

Here’s how I did it:

  1. Reinforce the new identity.
  2. Starve the old identity.

Reinforce the new identity

Look for confirming evidence

First off, find facts that fit with this new identity. Find times in your past when you acted in a way congruent with the identity. Find frames that support this new identity. Basically look for confirming evidence and arguments.

Take for example becoming chill about mosquitoes. I grew up in Canada, and during the summer the bugs could get quite bad. Especially working for my mountain man father in the Canadian wilderness, where I had to choose between two campsites: the one with bugs or the one with bears. (I chose bugs. I regretted this decision.)

I would usually get into a state of absolute misery. Every sensation was a potential bug on my skin. Every bite drove me closer to insanity.

But I wanted to overcome this. So I thought of the times it hadn’t bothered me. I thought of that summer night with a good friend where there were bugs but I was so caught up in the conversation I didn’t care.

I thought of new frames, like how my dad was never bothered by bugs. He said they were good for you. (Presuming you're in an area with no diseases carried by mosquitoes.)

And I thought of arguments: hunter gatherers presumably lived with mosquitoes their entire lives and weren’t being driven to madness over it. I was going to be living with mosquitoes for the rest of my life, and I didn't want to choose where I lived and traveled based on a tiny stupid bug.

(On a side note: I also solved mosquitoes. See here for the two pieces of equipment that remove practically all bites and itchiness.)

Make it social

So that’s step one. Another way to feed the new identity is to talk about it a lot. Tell friends and family about your new identity. Then the social pressure, even if just internally felt, helps you take it on. We are deeply social beings. Our identities are largely interpersonal. Use that.

Come up with a story of how you changed your identity

We live in self-narratives. Do it deliberately.

You can think “I’ve actually always been [new identity]”.

Another good one is to anchor it to a particular day. For example: "I was thinking about it one day, and I realized that actually, I'm going to be [new identity]."

For me, it was sitting out in the woods in the summer of 2020, getting bitten by a few mosquitoes. And I thought to myself: this is the day. I’m deciding to no longer be bothered by mosquitoes. And since then it’s been true.

Important: it has to be believable to you. If you don’t find it believable, it won’t work.

Pair it with strong emotions

We learn something more solidly if it’s paired with a strong emotion. PTSD is this mechanism running in the wrong direction: the lesson sticks forever because the fear was overwhelming. MDMA therapy is the same trick run in reverse. Emotional lessons stick more easily because they arrive wrapped in overwhelming feelings of love and safety.

Of course, therapeutic drugs are overkill for most identity changes. You can also just psych yourself up, invent a small ritual, or make the declaration somewhere awe inspiring, like the top of a mountain. This can help it stick long term.

Starve the previous identity

The biggest thing here is to simply not talk about the old identity. For example, whenever mosquitoes were around, I used to say “oh, I can’t stand mosquitoes. They drive me nuts.”

I stopped saying that. Out loud.

What about your internal thoughts? It's well established that you cannot suppress thoughts. Trying backfires. What you can do, though, is apply mindfulness when a thought from the old identity shows up. Acknowledge the thought, maybe give it a label (e.g. “there’s a thought” or “there’s the old identity”), then re-focus. Usually on whatever you're doing at the moment. Or, if you like, on the new identity and its story.

Important limitations to the technique

Like every psychological technique, this one doesn't work on everything. Some things about yourself are unchangeable. For example, I tried for years to be OK with polyamory and eventually had to admit that that was an aspect I couldn’t change about myself. Some things might have a cause that identity doesn’t affect, such as your environment or nutritional deficiencies.

So there you go. This is how you change your identity:

  • Reinforce the new identity
    • Look for confirming evidence and arguments
    • Talk about it
    • Come up with a narrative of how your identity changed
    • Pair it with strong emotions
  • Starve the old identity
    • Don’t talk about it
    • Acknowledge the thoughts, then re-focus

This is cross-posted from my Substack

item.title: Legal Personhood: an Unprotected AI Power Chokepoint
item.description:
Adapted from my Substack. This is the first installment of a series operationalizing the resilience program from AI as Normal Technology.

Epistemic status: Confident in the core thesis, less certain of its broader significance. The closing section says what would move me.

AI use: I used Claude Opus 5.5 for research, drafts, and review. I manually reviewed and redrafted every word in the final version dozens of times, retaining AI text only when I could not improve upon it.

Much of the AI risk conversation centers on questions nobody can answer yet: when superintelligence arrives, whether it will be aligned, whether a global regulatory regime can hold capabilities back. Meanwhile, some paths to power that today's AI can exploit are wide open, and the government could close them cheaply. The one we'll focus on here: in most of the US, you can form a company without anyone checking who (or what) you are.

North Korea already uses AI to fake identities, down to deepfaked job interviews, and researchers warn that AI agents could soon run whole shell networks with hardly a human in sight. The UK and Australia started verifying who runs their companies months or years ago. A few weeks ago, Washington doubled down on the loophole instead.

Companies are how AI can get a foothold in the economy. A human does business under a name they were born with and can't shed. A company is the only kind of legal person you can create on demand and throw away when it gets caught. That's what makes it a path to power that matters for AI.

AI doesn't have a birth certificate

Being smart doesn't give AI power on its own. To actually hold anything, from money and property to contracts and employees, an AI needs companies, bank accounts, and credentials that only humans provide. Even hacking only gets it in, and the hard part of a big theft has always been the cash-out, not the break-in.

For humans, paperwork is costly without AI help, while identity comes with being born. So the old system made paperwork the barrier and waved identity through on a signature. AI breaks this system because it can do paperwork at scale virtually for free, and it has no identity and nothing to lose.

But that very lack of identity is AI's biggest weakness. It can file a million shell companies, but it can't make a million people liable for them. Whether AI is a fraudster's tool or acting on its own, it has to cash out through a gate only humans should ever pass through. The fix at every gate to power comes down to two things:

  1. Identity: Verify and record an accountable human's personal information.
  2. Liability: Make sure that human pays if something goes wrong.

In 1968, economist Gary Becker pointed out that deterrence comes down to the chance of getting caught times the price of getting caught. Identity gives us a high chance, and liability gives us a high price. Get both right everywhere, and even very capable AI probably won't be able to quietly accumulate unaccountable power. The human accomplices it needs to recruit will recoil from getting involved, and the few who do it anyway will be shut down and prosecuted.

Right now, nobody checks who forms a company

You'd think registering a company would already require a verified human. It doesn't. Companies are formed under state law, and most states ask only for an organizer and a registered agent. Neither has to be an owner, and nobody checks ID. Most states don't even require you to list the owners. Banks check that the owners a company names are real people, but take the company's word that they're the ones in charge.

That used to be good enough, because faking an ownership structure across dozens of companies took real work. AI does that work for free.

This identity loophole doesn't just risk letting through unaccountable AI agents; it already causes plenty of damage today. It's what makes "phoenixing" work: fraudsters create a shell company, and when the bills come due, they dissolve the company and start a new one under a different name. "Chameleon carriers" in trucking do this to shed their safety violations while honest truckers have to pay for their mistakes.

Washington is unfortunately widening the identity loophole. In August, FinCEN permanently exempted every US-formed company from reporting who owns it, calling the requirement a burden on small business, and even announced it would delete the unverified records Americans had already filed.

Identity and liability close the loophole

The process of forming a company should run through our two principles of deterrence. Here's how it would work.

  1. Identity: At least one person who controls each company must verify their identity. For new companies, that happens at formation; for existing ones, within a year. A selfie and a photo of a license won't do, because AI can fake both. It has to be in person. The US Postal Service already provides in-person identity checks, and one visit gets you a verified login that covers every company you ever run. All we need now is the requirement.
  2. Liability: If the company vanishes to dodge fraud judgments or penalties, including ones handed down after it's gone, the verified person must pay them, and can't run another company until they do. Honest businesses that fail keep their protection, since ordinary debts stay with the company.

Nobody has to prove who's really in charge, because whoever verified pays. The obvious fraudster workaround is a straw owner: pay some human to put their name on it. But that human now has to show up in person, so stolen and fake identities stop working. Every front is a real person investigators can find. Knowingly fronting for fraud should mean prison, not just a debt the front will never pay. Any one gate can be slipped, but AI can only print paperwork for free; it can't print people.

None of this is new. On the identity side, the UK now requires every new company director to verify their identity, for free. Australia has required verified director IDs since 2021, specifically to stop phoenixing. Our version should insist on checks AI can't fake, but the principle is proven. Congress can do it nationally, since a federal appeals court upheld its power to require ownership disclosure. States can also act on their own. On the liability side, the IRS already makes the people running a company personally pay withheld payroll taxes they willfully fail to turn over.

We don't need new solutions. We need to act on the ones that already exist.

Identity and liability block other AI risks, too

The principles of identity and liability also cover other economic chokepoints, like payment rails.[1] They even help against hacking, because they play a critical role in getting powerful AI to cyber defenders first. Anthropic has given a select group of defenders privileged access to its most powerful model, and runs a verification program so legitimate security professionals can keep using its models as new safeguards arrive. The faster we can reliably verify defenders, the more secure our systems will be when attackers inevitably figure out how to use advanced AI agents maliciously. Anthropic shouldn't have to solve this alone.

A different risk arises when legitimate people and companies hand AI power willingly. There, the emphasis shifts from identity to liability. We’ll dig into that in the next installment.

How to cope with uncertain times

I don't know if or how superintelligence will work, and neither does anyone else. The right response is a saying made famous by Deng Xiaoping: "crossing the river by feeling the stones." We act on what we can see, watch what happens, and adjust. If verified identity keeps cyber defense ahead of offense and suppresses corporate and financial fraud, that's reason for optimism that the accountability principle stretches a long way. If AI finds paths to power that never touch an accountable person, or it works mostly through voluntary delegation in the legitimate economy, that's cause for concern and different controls.

Either way, this is worth doing. It stops fraud we already have, it's cheap, and it closes a loophole AI can easily exploit. That's the kind of fix we should be lining up now, instead of waiting for a crisis to scare us into knee-jerk measures that solve nothing.

When ChatGPT made a decent essay free and instant, the fix that worked was the blue book and the oral exam: colleges moving the test to something AI can't fake. The same trick will help AI-proof cyberspace and the economy.

Thanks to Abi Olvera and Arvind Narayanan for helpful pre-publication reviews, and to AI as Normal Technology for the profound reframing of AI safety that inspired this piece.

  1. ^

    Cryptocurrency should not be an exception to this. Anyone can hold crypto without an ID check, but spending it on anything important should require one, just as big cash payments already do. The principles of identity and liability don't work in an unregulated financial system, and that is a decisive argument against an unregulated financial system.

item.title: Athletic education vs. athletic torment
item.description:
I don’t know if it occurred to me until my thirties to think of exercise as an enjoyable thing. I was familiar with finding obscure corner-cases that were fun, such as Dance Dance Revolution. But the idea of it just often being a good time was alien.

I hesitate to blame anyone for anything, but school seems culpable here. I got the impression so firmly that PE class (‘physical education’ or ‘physed’) was a kind of horror, I’m not sure I would have treated this fact as on less solid ground than ‘you’re supposed to put a methods section in your lab report’. It just seemed like the way of things.

For children like me, anyway. Some children liked PE, but those were a totally different kind of creature. What the PE telos included was being awful for nerdy children, maybe to punish them for not being jocklike children. Since nerd children generally like not being jocks, they do not take this punishment as any serious feedback on their way of being, and just nobly withstand it. This is the way it is meant to be, and so it goes for every nerd until they break happily free and never play sports again. So was my rough picture of the situation, if I recall.

So this seems to mark a failure on the part of the schools: couldn’t they have at least got the message to me that this wasn’t the intended narrative, if it wasn’t?

But also, looking at the teaching methods, they don’t seem clearly distinguishable from what one might do if trying to traumatize non-athletic children:

  • Take all the children, with varying pre-existing levels of athletic skill and mortification about their bodies, and get them to change into different and skimpier outfits in front of each other.
  • Put them in ‘teams’. This ensures that when one of them does badly at the task, they are letting down half of their classmates (people whose social training so far consists largely of surviving and enacting schoolyard social dynamics, so their handling of this is unlikely to be ideally empathetic and graceful.)
  • Make multiple teams, so while half the class is disappointed by a child’s failure, the other half has a positive stake in it and may cheer the child on contemptuously. This might help teach the child to distrust positivity directed toward them, and respond to praise with stress and doubt rather than accepting it naively.
  • Traipse the group around outside shouting things and giving some people roles and authorities. Don’t clearly explain anything so that the whole class can hear it. Make reference to things that nerds won’t remember from previous sports classes.
  • Pick a task that is a) physically embarrassing to attempt in front of people if you are unathletic or overweight, b) at a level of difficulty that the least athletic classmates will find impossible and the most athletic will make look extremely easy, and c) allows for a chunk of the class to watch in real time and common knowledge as people fail
  • Do the activity for a vaguely disclosed period of time. If the nerds seem discouraged or confused, shout things they won’t understand.
  • Repeat at regular intervals.

(Not all of these elements were true in my own education, and probably few all of the time, but I think they are all recognizable.)

I’m guessing from the athletic child standpoint, this is a perfectly reasonable way to be taught that exercise is fun, and the teachers are mostly focused on maintaining that success rather than mitigating the losses with the children who are never going to excel there anyway. But I feel like they could have done so much better, especially if the purpose is in fact to educate the bulk of the students about physical activity, rather than for instance to scout out the student who might make it in professional sports. If it’s not, I think something like that would be cool to have in schools: a class that teaches all students about how to get exercise well and enjoyably.



Discuss

item.title: On Social Reality in China
item.description:
[Epistemic status: intuitions and anecdotes.]

Recently, several posts and projects (Thoughts Memo, Babel Translation, Please Give Them a Chance) have taken important steps towards raising AI safety awareness and sharing rationalist philosophy in China. It’s great that we’re recognizing the importance of solving the messaging problem for China, and thus laying the groundwork for an international AI pause. Below I record my perspective on cultural differences which are relatively underdiscussed, which may become roadblocks to this communication program.

Background: I’m a “first-generation” Chinese-American who moved to the States at the age of four. The beliefs in this essay are primarily drawn from interactions with my parents and their generation of immigrants, and from consumption of Chinese media (dramas, webnovels, games, and manhua) which are not necessarily representative of the realities on the ground. I am likely over-indexed on the older generation and internet culture, and would appreciate corrections from folks who have direct lived experience. The picture I aim to paint is also complicated by a massive generational gap, and my understanding is that some of the below sentiments (e.g. the cynicism and nationalism) are partly inherited by the younger generation, and partly rejected through a variety of countercultures.

Briefly, I point to four axes along which China is strikingly different. These differences are not black-and-white, but I think if you take the liberal middle-class western bubble I live in and shift the mode ~1 standard deviation in these directions you would get a substantively more accurate model of China:

  1. Chinese social media is like American junk food. Chinese people find American food disgusting: inauthentic slop inundated with additives and high fructose corn syrup. Westerners will find Chinese social media similarly disgusting: uncanny-valley filters are everywhere, and social media is omnipresent in every corner of life.
  2. Primacy of social reality, and of shame and “face.” Shame is seen as something that just works in China, and is the dominant lever by which virtue is enforced.
  3. Dark World thinking as described in Truth or Dare – a deep cynicism about human nature. People are by default out to get you. Emphasis on strength/competence and de-emphasis on kindness/virtue. Closely related to, but distinct from, scarcity mindset.
  4. Chinese nationalism as collective insecurity. The narrative is that China experienced a “century of humiliation” being brought to its knees by western colonizers, the Opium War, and Japanese atrocities in WW2, and the world still sees Chinese as “East Asian weaklings.” Through this lens, the primary drive of Chinese people is to prove themselves equal or superior to westerners and usher in the Chinese century.

Chinese Social Media is like American Junk Food

One thing I was shocked by when visiting China is that my grandparents went down to the supermarket every afternoon to buy fresh veggies to cook dinner. Chinese people, at least the older generation, are extremely careful about what they ingest, and have extremely high standards about freshness and culinary discernment. The idea of Americans storing fruit, veggies, and preserved food from the grocery store for weeks in the fridge is repulsive to them.

I think the exact reverse of this dynamic exists for social reality. Chinese beauty filters are out of control. Similarly, here’s what much of pre-AI manhuas look like:

Left to right: 重生都市天尊; 都市仙王; 最强仙尊陈北玄; 武炼巅峰.

Westerners sometimes tell a story that China embraces AI because of some philosophical positivity towards technological progress. I don’t entirely discount this story, but my impression is that Chinese consumers already had a high tolerance for slop and AI content fit naturally into this ecosystem without ever triggering an uncanny-valley reflex. If anything, AI slop is of higher quality than some of the existing mass-produced content. According to this article, one new AI mini-drama (several hours in length) launches every 36 seconds on Douyin.

Another striking feature of Chinese media is the ever-presence of audience reactions and the surrounding cultural conversation. Here is what I see if I pull up the first episode of idol drama “Pursuit of Jade” with 弹幕 (bullet comments) on by default:

Here’s the first chapter of a randomly-selected popular novel on Qidian (the largest site for Chinese webnovels):

See for yourself: Qidian chapter.

Every sentence is annotated with reader comments – so interacting with the reactions of other netizens is now part of the reading experience. Often these comments are filled with memes and in-jokes (梗) which take years of internet immersion to understand. And thus reading a novel, something I classify as one of the most private experiences, is embedded into the cultural conversation.

There is a lot more I could say: writing is filled with “clickbait” attention-grabbers; astroturfing and doxxing are entrenched industries; and it is typical for important events in slop novels to be padded by pages of fictional “social media reactions” showcasing in-universe virality. The basic message is: how others react to something is as important as the thing itself.

The Primacy of Social Reality

Here is the first verse of a popular children’s song:

小嘛小儿郎
背着那书包上学堂
不怕太阳晒
也不怕那风雨狂
只怕先生骂我懒哪
没有学问啰无颜见爹娘
朗里格朗里呀朗格里格朗
没有学问啰无颜见爹娘

I'm a small student.
I carry my backpack to school
I’m not afraid of the sun.
I’m also not afraid of the wind or the rain.
I'm only afraid that my teacher would scold me for being lazy
I'd lose face before my parents without the knowledge of school
Lan lee eh lan lan lee eh lan lan lee eh lan
I'd lose face before my parents without the knowledge of school.

This basic message is inculcated throughout Chinese upbringing: push through and ignore physical discomfort, but attend to and be subject to social censure. It’s okay to be buffeted by the elements, but if your grades are bad, you’ll be too ashamed to face your parents.

China lives inside an intricate and cynical theory of social reality. I wish I had some good writeups of this to point to; something that comes close is 48 Laws of Power, which cries out “this writer is sourcing from Chinese philosophy” but goes too far in the nuance-less sociopath manifesto direction.

To give some examples, the phrase 社死, “social death,” which means being so embarrassed that one might as well be dead socially, has gained a lot of popularity. I think there is a genuine sense in which people (everywhere, but more so in China) are more viscerally afraid of humiliation than death. (Again, there exists a nuanced dialectic about this phrase, and it is now used mostly ironically to joke about minor embarrassment. Further, many fictional protagonists are written as bold iconoclasts who do what is right despite social censure. I think this example still points to a culture preoccupied with social grace.)

Another example, as depicted in media, is a complex of subtle and entrenched rules “潜规则” (lit. “unspoken rules” or “underwater rules”) about social/corporate power that serve to enforce dominance hierarchies. The most salient such rule is “sleep with your boss to get ahead,” but more broadly, it points to dynamics like bribery and nepotism. Depending on status dynamics, being late is either a faux pas or a power move. Similarly with refusing to get drunk at a work dinner.

The Dark World Frame

A lot of anti-social behavior I used to intuitively attribute to "Dark Triad" pathologies – narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy – I now attribute to a cluster of cynical/self-defensive beliefs that Duncan Sabien identifies in Truth or Dare as “The Dark World frame.”

Dark World thinking is typified by Peter Thiel’s recent viral quote: “If you’re evil, at least you’re not bad.” Dark World thinking is everywhere, but in my experience there’s a particularly brazen strain in China. Key tenets of the Dark World:

No good deed goes unpunished.

It is better to be strong than good.

It is better to be evil than weak.

It is better to be honest than kind.

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

That which can be destroyed should be.

Kindness to others is cruelty to oneself.

A common trope in Chinese stories is what I call parenting-by-cauterization. A cruel master forces a young boy to kill his best friend: “He was your greatest weakness, kill him and you have one fewer.” Forming attachments is weakness. Breaking attachments makes you strong. (To be fair, this pattern is usually attributed to antagonists, and generally rejected as needlessly cruel by the overarching plot. My reading is that this is a real dialectic-in-progress to reject a pattern of generational trauma.)

Dark World thinking sees all virtue and kindness as pretense. Among many such tropes, a common derogatory trope is of women who act nice and innocent 白莲花 (white lotus) while being deceitful and manipulative on the inside. Chinese media creates trapped priors that people acting kind, altruistic, and pure are more likely to be evil. Similarly, the phrase 圣母 (Virgin Mary) is derogatory slang for someone who displays excessive (read: normal-to-westerners) levels of empathy. If all kindness is pretense and deceit, the only way to signal trustworthiness is cruelty. My father used to say, “Everyone will be nice to you, but only your family will be honest.”

One time I was having lunch with my wife and a Chinese friend, and the conversation meandered to why my wife entered college as a premed in her distant past life. Among the many reasons – money, respectability, parental approval – my wife brought up the motivation of “saving lives and helping people.” My friend laughed open-mouthed at that suggestion, taking it as an obvious joke. (Again, I don’t mean to say this person is representative of China. I suspect that their reaction is two-standard-deviations more Dark-World than the mode in China, and three-standard-deviations more Dark-World than the mode in the West.)

Zvi Mowshowitz once wrote a book review of The Three-Body Problem, where his thesis was “The real aliens are the Chinese people”:

Instead, the humans are written a lot stranger, to my American eyes, than the Trisolarians. Most characters are Chinese, but even those who are not continue to mostly think and act in this similarly alien style. I appreciated the opportunity to see the view of humanity from someone in a completely different culture. But it points out how ordinary the Trisolarians are that they are, at least, not obviously less like the humans I know, than are the humans in the book. How much of this is how the Chinese or some Chinese group view humans and think about the world, versus how the author does? I cannot say.

The viewpoint expressed is deeply, deeply conservative and cynical.

People, all but a handful of them, are absurdly fickle, petty, short-sighted, self-interested and self-defeating. They are obsessed with status and how they are relative to others, and on the margin wish others harm rather than well. If anyone tries to escape disaster or otherwise rise on their own, universally mankind's response is to band together to kill them.

The Three-Body Problem is a particularly extreme example of the Dark World frame, and it’s an outlier because science fiction is grim-dark by default. My guess is that half of the Dark-Worldness of The Three-Body Problem derives from the nature of science fiction, and half from Chinese culture. There’s a reason the second book is called The Dark Forest.

Chinese nationalism as collective insecurity

At some point I was watching American Ninja Warrior, and one season hosted national teams from various countries. When the interviewer came around to hear people’s stories, all the western teams were like “I’m doing this to set a good example for my wife and kids at home.” The Chinese team was like “I’m doing this to prove to the world that Chinese people can be great athletes.”

In 2025 we saw the launch of an absolutely peak FMV game “Road to Empress” about instrumental convergence a fictionalized account of China’s only official female ruler Wu Zetian. Ludwig went viral in China for streaming it on Twitch, to the extent that the creators flew him out to China to film a cameo in the sequel:

Ludwig’s cameo.

The top comment on the Bilibili playthrough, which Ludwig reacted to in this clip, went, “This game is really good-looking. It can let foreigners know that Asians are not all squinty-eyed as in the stereotype [grin] There are also many handsome men and beautiful women.” Ludwig’s response was “I'm laughing that their idea of America is that before playing this game, I thought all people in Asia were the stereotype with the squinty eyes.”

Even among strains of nationalism, Chinese nationalism seems to be particularly chip-on-your-shoulder. My impression is that this kind of insecurity is less in your face, but still present, in younger Chinese today. It is concerning how much Chinese AI models catching up in the AI race is entangled with this national insecurity.

—

The point of this post is to open for the reader my fairly narrow window into Chinese culture, and to draw attention to certain features I find alien as an American.

I suspect that if the rationalist project wants to take root in China, it has to solve problems like not being immediately branded as holier-than-thou “圣母”, and adjusting to the cutthroat attention economy of Chinese social media. HPMOR is an example of something (grimdark power-scaling quasi-isekai fantasy) that likely appeals to Chinese netizens; Peter Singer is not.

I like to say that if LessWrong is “on the spectrum” and “more autistic than normal,” where normal is set to the ambient western culture, then China lives past the right endpoint of the spectrum, at “even more allistic than normal.” My current hypothesis is that the locally optimal message to China is in the vein of “give us your autists who feel alienated by the monoculture,” but others may prefer a more conciliatory approach that directly appeals to the dominant culture.



Discuss

item.title: Book Review: Obsolete
item.description:
Book review: Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion Dollar Race to Replace Us? and How to Stop It, by Garrison Lovely.

Obsolete is a strange book. It’s mostly good, but the quality varies a good deal. Lovely is well informed about concerns that AI might kill us all, and doesn’t dispute those concerns. Yet he focuses much more on more ordinary concerns, in particular excessive concentration of power.

He is somewhat successful at portraying mundane harms of this year, and longer term risks (will AI kill us all in the 2030s), as similar problems. I usually cringe at such efforts, but Lovely is quite good at defusing the tensions between those two types of concern. E.g. he discusses AI-assisted political coups by a CEO such as Musk in a way that sounds almost realistic using current AI, while also warning about dramatic increases in that risk as AI becomes more powerful.

Most of the book is written for a pretty broad audience. I’m annoyed that he added in a modest number of gratuitous culture war quips that will repel some Republicans. He mitigates that a little by also complaining about widespread corruption among leading Democrats, but many Republicans won’t read far enough to notice that.

Obsolete also contains a few distracting sections on topics such as how to improve drug development. That passage would make an excellent blog post, but feels quite out of place in the middle of policy advice for dealing with AI risks.

Two examples of Lovely describing his concerns well:

He answers the “can’t you just unplug it” question by pointing to OpenAI’s inability to unplug a rogue CEO in November 2023.

He shows the Andy Jones chart of the horse population with a nearly 90% drop between 1930 and 1950.

For the first 120 years of that steady improvement, horses didn’t notice at all. … Progress in engines was steady. Equivalence to horses was sudden.

China

Lovely is correct to report that AI companies aren’t very good at keeping secrets, but he overstates how much that matters:

All of this means slowing US frontier software progress, via regulation or other means, wouldn’t hand China a lead it couldn’t otherwise achieve; it would slow the entire pack.

Copying US AI is not the main source of Chinese AI progress. This is an area with much disagreement among experts. Distillation is real, but overrated. My guess is that at least half of Chinese AI progress is due to there being plenty of low hanging fruit that many experts can find. Chinese companies face different constraints than US companies due to restrictions on selling compute to China. Chinese companies have adapted to their compute scarcity by focusing on performance optimizations that were lower priority for US companies. That means there were some medium-value respects in which China has led the US. See Aidan Gomez, Kyle Chan, and Min et alfor more thorough arguments.

On the other hand, Lovely underestimates how willing the Chinese government would be to slow an AI capabilities race if there were enough evidence to convince Trump to do the same. They’re not very eager to race toward superintelligence. Instead, they’re racing toward widespread deployment of AI applications such as robotics, which is where they have an advantage over the US.

AI’s China hawks – Altman and Amodei – are right about one thing: there is a titanic struggle over who controls the future. But it’s not between democracies and autocracies, it’s between humanity and them.

There are multiple struggles over AI. Lovely oversimplifies here. I want encourage more cooperative approaches to handling AI. I worry about Lovely encouraging conflict.

Antitrust

One of Lovely’s policy prescriptions starts with the great title “Too big to guardrail”. But he mostly wants to make AI companies smaller by using antitrust law.

Antitrust action to break up Nvidia or TSMC could make AI more affordable to the average person, more affordable to companies that want to replace human workers with AIs, and could help ensure that many nations have drone armies, rather than drone armies being concentrated in a smaller number of powerful nations. Those seem like mostly the opposite of what Lovely and I want.

Lovely seems more focused on breaking up Anthropic and OpenAI. But antitrust seems like the wrong tool here. Much of what concerns me about those two are the reckless competition between them that closely matches what antitrust law promotes.

Maybe Lovely has a good idea about how to make AI companies smaller, but he sure failed to communicate it here.

How Obsolete is the Book?

AI and the political landscape around it have changed frequently in the 6 months between when Lovely finished writing the book and publication. Most authors would have several claims about AI that got falsified in that time period. Roughly none of Lovely’s claims about what AIs do have been discredited, partly because he minimizes his reliance on claims about what AI can and can’t do.

Lovely has more mixed success at predicting what humans would do, but still looks pretty good.

If you model OpenAI as an organization trying to use AI to improve the world, you’ll be left confused by decisions like [releasing Sora]. But if you model it like Netflix or Meta – as another company trying to maximize its ownership share in all human attention – everything makes sense.

A month after Lovely finished writing the book, OpenAI shut down Sora. Apparently, owning much of our attention isn’t very valuable compared to what OpenAI is prioritizing now.

Anthropic’s alignment strategy simply wasn’t robust to a would-be despot taking the White House, even though it had already fucking happened.

This seems to refer to the Supply Chain Risk designation. I’d say Anthropic’s strategy worked as well as we could hope for, unlike some of its competitors.

Senator Bernie Sanders offered one answer in late 2025: a moratorium on data center construction in the US. In a world of half-measures, his proposal embodies the ambition needed to meet the moment.

Lovely proceeds in the next few paragraphs to mostly admit that the 2025 proposal was an inadequate half-measure. But he was partly prophetic, in that Sanders introduced a sufficiently ambitious bill just before Obsolete was published.

Lovely went out on a limb when he reported the beginnings of AI-related job losses, based on what was then rather thin evidence. Economists this month say the evidence has gotten stronger.

The tone of Obsolete seems optimized for public opinion as of when Lovely wrote it. Opinions are now more focused on loss of control:

Concluding Thoughts

This book will both increase understanding of why we should be concerned about AI, and push the US a little closer to turning AI into a tribal issue. I estimate an 80% chance that the book will have net positive effects.

More quotes:

When it’s deployed, the advanced agent is deliberately trying to capture the company that built it the way a corporation tries to capture a regulator.

Against standard inferences from the METR time horizon results:

Writing this book has been harder than all my other writing combined. As a piece gets longer, it gets exponentially harder to work on. … while much of the writing and reporting I’ve done over my career helped me write the book, many of the skills I needed to learn happened only over the course of writing the book itself.



Discuss

item.title: Evaluating the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act
item.description:
MIRI recently endorsed the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, but others like ControlAI have called it overly broad, and a few other respected experts have outright endorsed it in its current form.

I decided to take a look at it myself and see both what the bid is trying to do and whether it actually does it well.

The goal of this act is to ban any AI that shows traits that indicate it could cause great harm to society, and to restrict the development of advanced AI to certified institutions who can be trusted to do so safely. This seems like a reasonable goal.

The problem with this bill, as far as I can see it, isn't that its goal is wrong, but that the way it's been drafted contains lots of flaws, which are likely to have unintended negative consequences.

At it's core, the bill does four things:

  • Ban AI that has one of six dangerous capabilities
    • Automate or greatly accelerate AI research and development
    • Access secured systems without authorization
    • Keep operating despite attempts to shut it down
    • Meaningfully help with nuclear, chemical, or biological weapons
    • Modify its own functions
    • Scheme, deceive, or avoid human oversight
  • Only allow certified orgs to train “Advanced AI Systems” - An advanced AI system is defined as any model that has been trained with greater than 10^25 operations. Only certified orgs are allowed to develop such models. As such, they are the only people allowed to posses an advanced AI system that has not yet been certified as safe.
  • Establish a government department tasked with certifying that an AI system is safe - No Advanced AI System can be distributed unless it has received certification from this department.
  • Impose strict penalties for people who recklessly distribute dangerous AI - Up to 20 years in prison and the forfeiture of all assets of a business.

This basic framework seems broadly sensible, although there are legitimate questions about the extent to which we want to ban the automation of AI research, whether this gives the government too much control, and whether it limiting distribution of pre-approved models might make AI safety research harder.


The biggest problem with the bill is that, as currently drafted, it would have lots of negative consequences. In particular:

  • The dangerous capabilities rules are vaguely defined, and they come into force immediately, without waiting for them to be clarified - This makes it hard to know what is actually illegal. A bill would normally be expected to task the department with coming up with a clear testing standard, and require that standard to be agreed before people could be punished for violating it.
  • Existing models are not grandfathered in - You’d expect all models prior to the enactment of the bill to be declared legal to avoid chaos - maybe with some regime for distributing signatures for permitted models. As drafted, it seems that existing models might be illegal to possess or distribute, and there initially isn’t any way to know what is legal.
  • The dangerous capability rules appear to apply to any AI, not just advanced AI - I suspect that they had intended the rules to only apply to advanced AI systems (those that take more than 10^25 operations to train and require approval before release), but that is not the way the bill is written. Smaller open source models become a legal grey area because there is no requirement that they be certified as legal, but the law still applies. Indeed, since the bill doesn't define AI, or a threshold for its banned capabilities, a particularly pedantic reading of the bill could argue that a calculator or online textbook were illegal.
  • It punishes looking for danger - If you look for risks and you find one, you are now in possession of a banned model and face harsh penalties. A law would normally provide safe harbor for safety research. Nobody is required to check for precursors and there would now be a big incentive not to.
  • All development of advanced AI pauses until the department is fully staffed and has finalized its rules, with no timeline for doing that - The department has no budget and would likely take a while to ramp up. This would mean an indefinite shutdown of US AI labs and thus likely a migration of their research to other countries during that period of uncertainty.
  • The “Advanced AI Systems” threshold is sufficiently low to include GPT4 and other old models - The bill is unclear, but a strict reading would say that it is illegal to distribute all current US frontier models - because they are "advanced AI systems" and have not yet been certified by the government as safe.
  • It potentially makes mutual agreement with China much harder - The main leverage we have with China is that the US is currently ahead in AI. If the US was not ahead in AI then that leverage would be lost. 
  • The limit of 10^25 training operations is hard to enforce and likely will be gamed - This wouldn’t matter so much if it was just the point at which sensible regulation come into play (e.g. for some of the other bills), but matters a lot if larger models are essentially banned. Companies will be dishonest about their degree of training, or bypass it by putting more effort into algorithmically generated training data that gives a model a smooth path to training to the desired shape.


My overall sense is that what this bill is trying to do is broadly sensible, and it has the potential to turn into a good bill with a bit of editing, but it is not a good bill in it's current form. This is something of a shame, because I worry that, in a way reminiscent of the Toxoplasma of Rage the bill in its current form becomes the main way people argue about more strictly limiting the development of superintelligent AI, making it harder for a better bill to emerge.





Discuss

item.title: Do you understand what I mean when I say “existential risk”?
item.description:
By the end of this post, I hope you’ll take existential risk more seriously. I hope you will feel as viscerally as I do the stakes of human survival and flourishing.

When I tell people, “I think AI is an existential risk”, usually nothing changes about their expression. They nod along, same blank face, thinking about what they’re going to have for lunch today. I want to take them by the shoulders and shake them and ask, “Are you listening? Do you know what I mean when I say ‘existential risk’? Why do you accept what I say so passively?”

When I say existential risk, I’m talking about outcomes that curtail humanity’s development forever — human extinction, permanent totalitarianism, or some crippling catastrophe that we can’t rebuild civilization up from. Do you understand, in your heart, the stakes of this?

I think when I talk about existential risk, particularly human extinction, it doesn’t feel real to people. The words “existential risk” glide in one ear and out the other — an interesting idea to consider, but abstract compared to the pressing issues today.

Let me say: existential risk is real and possible. I’m going to focus on extinction as an outcome that’s most salient to me.

99% of species that have ever lived have gone extinct. Humanity, too, can just go extinct. We can all die. This is possible! There is no force of the universe, by my eyes, that protects us. There is no rescuer, no mother or father, who will magically swoop in to save us in our time of need. It is possible for us to exist — and then one day, not. The world was barren of meaning before we existed; the world can be barren once again.

Let me clarify as well that human extinction is bad. It’s easy to hear human extinction and feel ambivalent. You imagine a peaceful end, a blink and then nothingness. What’s so special about humans, after all? Earth rotates without us — oh well.

But let’s be for real. You hear that an asteroid is hurtling toward Earth right now, and that it has a 10% chance of killing us all. Seriously, imagine that for 5 seconds. Your mom calls you to tell you the news. There’s a tremor in her voice. Word spreads quickly — the air is solemn on campus, or at work. National leaders congregate to figure out what to do. The best scientists across the globe are working day and night, but they’re uncertain if it’s enough. You look around for ways you can help — can you do research? can you make the scientists’ lives easier? can you be a source of stability for your loved ones? Some of your friends have decided that they can’t do anything, that they’re better off just enjoying their life and ignoring the problem. You don’t understand them. In the end, they’ll wish they did more.

Humanity is a flame, the only light in this world. We may be unique in our capacity for moral reasoning, our ability to fight against the “‘is-ness’ of man’s present nature” and aspire for the “eternal ‘ought-ness’”. We have transformed the world, both for worse and for better. But if we die, there is no chance for things to ultimately improve, to supersede the neutrality of nature. If we die, who knows how long it will take for there to exist another species that can take our place, that can feel joy and sorrow and love like us? The flame is precious, and only we can protect it.
